Home, plans, downtime and arguments — how well you match in everyday life.
For now you walk side by side, but each on your own route. Start small: half an hour a day without phones and a talk about the week ahead.
You have a solid base, but daily life and plans sometimes drift apart. Agree on the small things — those hold a couple together, not the big dates.
You read each other well, both at home and in your plans. Keep the habit of talking things through instead of guessing.

Time, gifts, words, care and touch: how you say “I love you”.
It seems you still speak different languages and wait for the other to guess. Start with one simple question: what matters most to your partner?
You feel each other, but little gestures sometimes get lost in the daily rush. Add one small action a day — the effect shows up fast.
You speak your partner\'s language and don\'t forget it in daily life. That is a rare skill — protect it and keep it fed.
Do you know your partner\'s love language?
Yes, and I try to speak it

Directly: “I miss you”, “you matter to me”

Only when someone is really tired
A fun quiz about your couple\'s habits: who makes up first, who forgets the keys and who comes up with plans.
It looks like your habits run a bit in parallel. There aren\'t many funny shared rituals yet — a good time to start a couple of your own.
Half your habits are shared, half are your own. That\'s fine: what matters is that you notice them and can laugh together.
You are very much a pair: even the little things are shared. A great foundation — just don\'t forget to surprise each other now and then.

Chores, the shared budget, savings and purchases — how your everyday life works.
Home and money still run on their own for you, and that tires you both. Start with one step: five minutes a week on “who does what” and “what we spent”.
You have a base, but the agreements rest on memory, not rules. Write down who does what and a limit for big purchases — things will feel calmer.
You run your home and budget as a team: you talk, plan and don\'t build up grudges. That is the strongest part of a couple — protect it.

Home, work, holidays and five-year dreams: are you looking the same way?
You hardly talk about the future, and each of you pictures it alone. Start with one question: “How do you see our next year?” — no debates, no deadlines.
You know the important things about each other, but you discuss plans more than you write them down. One shared goal for six months will make the talks more concrete.
You share a picture of the future and a habit of checking it. That is a rare match — keep dreaming out loud.
